common_name: White Cup and Saucer Vine (Cobaea Alba)

planting.note: Start seeds indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost, standing the large flat seeds on edge in moist compost rather than laying them flat, since this reduces rot; provide bottom heat to speed germination.

directions: This is a pure white-flowered selection of cup and saucer vine, distinguished from the species by blooms that stay creamy white rather than aging to deep purple. Sow seed on edge indoors well ahead of the last frost, since it needs a long season to reach its vigorous mature size. Once transplanted after frost danger has passed, give it a sturdy trellis, arbor, or fence, as the clinging tendrils allow it to climb quickly to considerable height in a single season. Its large, fragrant, bell-shaped flowers open against a leafy green calyx and continue from midsummer until frost; in zones 9-11 it can persist as a short-lived perennial.

planting.note: Start seeds indoors 10-12 weeks before last frost at warm temperatures; this selection, developed at Tresco Abbey Garden in the Isles of Scilly, is grown exactly as the species and begins flowering within a few months of sowing.

directions: Tresco Scarlet is a named selection of Chilean glory flower bred for consistently rich scarlet-orange tubular blooms rather than the more variable orange-red of open-pollinated seed. Sow indoors well before the last frost, since germination and establishment are slow, then transplant into a warm, sheltered, sunny spot with a trellis, fence, or shrub to climb through via its grasping leaf tendrils. It grows extremely fast once warm weather arrives, flowering continuously into autumn, and in mild coastal climates within zones 8-10 it survives winter as a woody-based perennial. In colder zones treat it as a fast, showy annual climber.

common_name: White Bengal Clock Vine (Alba Sky Vine)

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings or container specimens in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after all frost danger has passed; like the species, this white-flowered form grows extremely rapidly and needs a very sturdy, large trellis, pergola, or fence to support it, and is considered invasive in parts of Florida and Hawaii, so avoid planting near natural areas.

directions: This is a pure white-flowered form of the vigorous Bengal clock vine, otherwise identical to the species in habit and cultural needs. Propagate from stem cuttings rooted in warm, moist medium, since it is typically grown from vegetative starts rather than seed. Once established against a strong support, it climbs aggressively by twining stems and produces large clusters of trumpet-shaped white flowers with pale yellow throats through the warm months. In zones 9-11 it persists as a woody perennial vine and should be pruned hard after flowering to control its size; in cooler zones grow it as a container specimen brought indoors before frost.

planting.note: Start indoors 4-6 weeks before transplanting, soaking seeds overnight in warm water to improve germination; move to a trellis, hanging basket, or small obelisk after all frost danger has passed.

directions: Susie Yellow is a bright golden-yellow selection from the classic Susie seed strain, showing the same bold dark, near-black central throat that gives Black-Eyed Susan Vine its name. Start seed indoors on the same schedule as other Susie selections and transplant into a warm, sunny spot after frost, training the twining stems onto a trellis or letting them cascade from a hanging basket. It flowers continuously from early summer through the first frost and tolerates heat and humidity better than many other flowering annual vines. Pinch young plants to encourage branching and deadhead occasionally to keep flowering strong.
